notes.text: After — When that year ended, and the next begun, which was in the spring time. When kings - Which is, when the ground is fit for the march of soldiers, and brings forth provision for man and beast. Tarried at Jerusalem - Had he been now in his post, at the head of his forces be had been out of the way of temptation.

Arose from off his bed — Where he had lain, and slept for some time. And the bed of sloth often proves the bed of lust. Washing herself - In a bath, which was in her garden. Probably from some ceremonial pollution.

He inquired — Instead of suppressing that desire which the sight of his eyes had kindled, he seeks rather to feed it; and first inquires who she was; that if she were unmarried, he might make her either his wife or his concubine.
Took her — From her own house into his palace, not by force, but by persuasion. Lay with her - See how all the way to sin is down hill! When men begin, they cannot soon stop themselves.
Go down — Not doubting but he would there converse with his wife, and so cover their sin and shame.
The servants — With the king's guard. This he did, by the secret direction of God's wise providence, who would bring David's sin to light.
Camest — Wearied with hard service and travel, nor did I expect or desire that thou shouldest now attend upon my person, or keep the watch.

The ark — This it seems, was now carried with them for their encouragement and direction, as was usual. Fields - In tents which are in the fields. His meaning is, now, when God's people are in a doubtful and dangerous condition, it becomes me to sympathize with them, and to abstain even from lawful delights.

He arose — So far is David from repenting, that he seeks to cover one sin with another. How are the beginnings of sin to be dreaded! For who knows where it will end? David hath sinned, therefore Uriah must die! That innocent, valiant, gallant man, who was ready to die for his prince's honour, must die by his prince's hand! See how fleshly lusts war against the soul, and what devastations they make in that war! How they blind the eyes, fear the conscience, harden the heart, and destroy all sense of honour and justice!

glossa.text: *And it came to pass, at the return of the year, at the time when,* etc. ((RAB., ex Hieron.)) That is, in the spring, when, the harshness of the cold being driven away, fodder is found for the beasts of burden, etc., *as far as* but they were overcome.

*While these things.* ((RAB.)) David sinned grievously, etc., *as far as* who healed so grievous a wound of sin by the confession of humility.

*Bethsabee.* ((ISID.)) The well of fullness, or the seventh well. But the Church is called the well of living water, and to this well the name of the sevenfold number is joined in signification of the Holy Spirit, by reason of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven. To forty-nine, that is, to seven times seven, one is added, since unity is commended. Whence: *Careful to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace ((Eph. IV))*. And so by the spiritual gift, that is, by the sevenfold gift, the Church has been made the well of fullness, because there has been made in her *a fountain of water springing up into life everlasting, whereof he that shall drink shall not thirst for ever ((Joan. IV))*.

 ((GREG.)) Weighed down as we still are by the burden of corruptible flesh, we are not able so to live that no delight of guilt can beat upon us. But it is one thing to be touched unwillingly, and another to consent. But holy men keep themselves with a circumspection so much the more watchful, as they disdain to be beaten upon by sinister motions even in passing, so that, if perchance the heart should covet anything unlawful, the eye, restrained by the mastery of discipline, would refuse to see: for as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes what has been conceived within compels the eye without to serve it. For very often some thing or other is looked upon with an innocent mind, but in the very looking the soul is confounded by the sword of concupiscence. For David did not look upon the wife of Urias of set purpose because he had coveted her, but rather he coveted because he looked incautiously. But by the just examination of retribution, he who uses the outward eye negligently is blinded in the inward eye. But often concupiscence already lords it within, and the soul, enticed, exacts after the manner of a tyranny that the bodily senses be servants to its own uses, and compels the eyes to serve its own pleasures, and opens the windows of light unto the darkness of blindness. Whence holy men, when they feel themselves beaten upon with sinister delight, restrain by the mastery of discipline those very lights through which the appearance of a form enters into the mind, lest a seductive seeing should be a servant to a depraved thought: and if this is ever neglected to be subtly guarded, the uncleanness of thought passes over into action.

 ((GREG.)) Often some thing or other is a virtue in the history, a fault in the signification; just as sometimes a fault in the deed is a virtue in the writing of prophecy. For who would not detest that David, walking on the roof, coveted Bethsabee the wife of Urias, whom nevertheless, when he returned from the battle, he admonishes to go home and to wash his feet? And he straightway answered, saying: The ark of God is under skins, and shall I take my rest in my own house? Whom David received at his own table, and gave him the banquet through which he was to die. David therefore holds the figure of him of whom it is written: *He hath set his tabernacle in the sun ((Psal. XVIII))*. Who bids Bethsabee be brought forth to him, that is, to join to himself by a spiritual understanding the law of the letter that was joined to a carnal people. For Bethsabee is called *a well of seven*, because through the kinship of the law, by the pouring in of a special grace, perfect wisdom is ministered to us. But Urias signifies the Jewish people, who is interpreted *my light of God:* for the Jewish people, which is lifted up by the knowledge of the law it has received, glories as it were in the light of God. But David took away this man's wife and joined her to himself, because the Redeemer, appearing strong of hand, while he made known that the law speaks spiritually of himself, showed her to be a stranger to the Jewish people by that whereby they were held according to the letter, and joined her to himself, because he declared himself to be preached through her. Yet he admonishes Urias to go home and to wash his feet, because, being incarnate, he commands the Jews to return to their conscience, and to wipe away with weeping the filth of their works; that they may understand the commandments of the law spiritually, and, after so great a hardness of precepts, finding the fountain of baptism, may run to the water after their labour. But Urias, who remembers that the ark of the Lord is under skins, answers that he cannot enter his own house. Which is to say: I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to my conscience through spiritual understanding. For he says as it were that the ark of God is under skins, because he understands the precepts of God not otherwise than by performing the ministry of a carnal sacrifice. Yet David calls this man, who is unwilling to go home, to his table, because, while the Jews scorn to return to their conscience, Christ nevertheless preaches spiritual things, saying: *If you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote of me ((Joan. V))*. For the Jew holds the law, which speaks of his divinity, whom he disdains to believe. Whence Urias also is sent to Joab with letters by which he was to be slain, because the Jew carries the law by whose conviction he is to die. For while, holding fast the commandments of the law, he strives to fulfil them, he himself carries down the judgment whereby he is condemned. What therefore is more wicked than David by this deed? What more clean than Urias? But as to the mystery: what more holy than David? What more faithless than Urias? Because he, through the fault of his life, marks the innocence of prophecy; and this man, through the innocence of his life, expresses fault in prophecy. For the power of the sacred eloquence so narrates what is past that it expresses what is to come: so approves the thing in the deed that it contradicts it in the mystery. So it condemns things done, that it urges these same things to be done mystically.

*Set ye Urias,* etc. ((GREG., lib. XXXIII Moral., cap. 10.)) To this end are the sins of David and of Peter set down in Scripture, that the ruin of the greater may be the caution of the lesser, etc., *as far as* by a secret order of dispensation therefore, whence the iniquity of the devil is permitted to rage, thence the goodness of God is accomplished, because thence it obeys the biddings of supernal grace, whence it works the wrath of its own will.

notes.text: The fool — The wicked man. Good - That is, actions really good or pleasing to God.

Looked — God knoweth all things without any enquiry: but he speaks after the manner of men. Upon - Upon the whole Israelitish nation, and upon all mankind for he speaks of all except his people, and the righteous ones, who are opposed to these, ver. 4, 5.
Gone — From God, and from the rule which he hath given them. Filthy - Loathsome and abominable to God.
Bread — With as little remorse, and with as much greediness. Call not - They are guilty not only of gross injustice towards men, but also of horrid impiety and contempt of God.
There — Upon the spot, where they practiced these insolences, God struck them with a panick fear. For - God is on their side, and therefore their enemies have cause to tremble.
Because — This was the ground of their contempt, that he lived by faith in God's promise and providence.

O that — These words immediately concern the deliverance of Israel out of that sinful state, in which they now were; which having described, he concludes, with a prayer to God to help them out of Zion, where the ark then was, but principally they design the spiritual redemption and salvation of all God's Israel by the Messiah. The captivity - His captive people. The children of Jacob, as Aaron is named for his sons, 1 Chron. xii, 27. The scope of this short, but excellent psalm, is to shew us the way to heaven. Here is a question proposed, ver. 1. The answer to it, ver. 2-5. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The fool hath said.* ((CASS.)) A rebuke of the Jews, their malice being described. The first psalm concerning the rebuke of the Jews, etc., *as far as* this man is not God.

*The Lord from heaven. ((Ibid.))* But from thence they are without excuse, because the Lord looked down, that is, he stood forth out of human nature. ((AUG.)) From heaven, that is, he looks down through holy souls: for by himself nothing lies hidden from him. Or, from heaven, through holy souls, which are the heaven and the seat of God. Or, the Lord the Father from heaven, that is, from the secret of the divine mind. ((CAS.)) Or, from the equality of God the Father. *If there be one that understandeth.* Or, he saw whether there be one that understandeth, and he found that not one understands: because he does not seek, but turns aside, for: *All have gone aside,* etc.

*A sepulchre. ((Ibid.))* Thus made useless to others, because their throat is a sepulchre, etc. *A sepulchre.* These three verses, which run as far as the second division, at *Shall they not know,* etc., are said not to be from the Hebrew, etc., *as far as* it does not have them.

*Destruction* ((AUG.)) Thus they have been made useless to themselves, etc., *as far as* and unhappiness in the time to come.

(CASS) The way of the wicked, etc., *as far as: The fear of God before their eyes,* etc.
*Shall they not know.* He threatens judgment to the wicked.

*The Lord they have not called upon,* etc. ((AUG.)) For they do not truly call upon him who love the things that displease God.--((CASS.)) Thence destruction is increased, because they must needs do evil, since the proud will not call upon God. As it is caution to fear at the fitting time, so it is cowardice to tremble unfittingly, as for nation and place, the fear of God being cast away.
*The counsel of the needy.* ((CASS.)) An invective against the Jews, etc., *as far as,* that is, proceeding from the Jews, etc.

*Who shall give out of Sion,* etc. ((CASS.)) Last of all the conversion of the Jews is foretold, which will come to pass when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in. *When he shall have turned away.* For the Jews too the Apostle sets down this testimony of Isaiah: *There shall come out of Sion he that turneth away the captivity, or the impiety, from Jacob.*

notes.text: Of whom — The Father. The whole family of angels in heaven, saints in paradise, and believers on earth is named. Being the "children of God," (a more honourable title than "children of Abraham,") and depending on him as the Father of the family.
The riches of his glory — The immense fulness of his glorious wisdom, power, and mercy. The inner man - The soul.
Dwell — That is, constantly and sensibly abide.

That being rooted and grounded — That is, deeply fixed and firmly established, in love. Ye may comprehend - So far as an human mind is capable. What is the breadth of the love of Christ - Embracing all mankind. And length - From everlasting to everlasting. And depth - Not to be fathomed by any creature. And height - Not to be reached by any enemy.

And to know — But the apostle corrects himself, and immediately observes, it cannot be fully known. This only we know, that the love of Christ surpasses all knowledge. That ye may be filled - Which is the sum of all. With all the fulness of God - With all his light, love, wisdom, holiness, power, and glory. A perfection far beyond a bare freedom from sin.

Now to him — This doxology is admirably adapted to strengthen our faith, that we may not stagger at the great things the apostle has been praying for, as if they were too much for God to give, or for us to expect from him. That is able - Here is a most beautiful gradation. When he has given us exceeding, yea, abundant blessings, still we may ask for more. And he is able to do it. But we may think of more than we have asked. He is able to do this also. Yea, and above all this. Above all we ask - Above all we can think. Nay, exceedingly, abundantly above all that we can either ask or think.
In the church — On earth and in heaven.

glossa.text: *For this cause.* I entreat you, and I beseech God, that grace may work together with you. And this is what he adds: *For this cause.* In which he shows that they have the free choice of their own will. But lest they think that this suffices, he adds: *I bow my knees to the Father.* So much only is had in the Greek; but what has been added in the Latin codices: *of our Lord Jesus Christ,* fits well, in that he was praying that we might obtain by the merit of him to whom he is Father properly and naturally, and not by adoption.

*Fatherhood,* etc. Neither angel, nor man is truly a father as God is, who is the father of all by creation, and of the faithful by re-creation, whom he adopted as sons. Or *is named,* that is, is nameable. For from him who is the father of all, both the angels in heaven and men on earth received that they should call others fathers. And note that Christ, the only-begotten of God by nature, signifies by the benefit of adoption that he is a father, saying, *Son, thy sins are forgiven thee ((Matth. II))*. In like manner also the Holy Spirit, through whom the just are adopted as sons. But a man is called father either by nature, or by the authority of example, or by reason of benefit.
*In charity.* I pray also that [you may be] *rooted,* that is, firmly planted, from the likeness of a tree, which the more it is fixed in the earth, the more it grows, and yields a richer fruit.

*With all the saints.* This is the communion of the heavenly commonwealth. These seek not their own, but the things which are Christ's, that is, they pursue not private advantages, but take counsel in the communion where the salvation of all is.

*What is the breadth.* Of charity, which ought to be extended even to enemies, and to work well with cheerfulness, because he who gives sadly loses what he gives. There is need, therefore, of the breadth of charity, lest whatever good thou dost should perish. But because, iniquity abounding, the charity of many grows cold, there is need also of length.

*And sublimity.* Of charity. This is that the heart be directed upward, that God be awaited as the reward. For if thou workest well even toward enemies, and givest cheerfully, thou hast breadth; and if in these things unto the end thou perseverest, thou hast length. But if thou do all these things not for the sake of the heavenly reward, it has not height: and so now there will be neither breadth nor length. For to have height is to think God, to love God, and freely to love him the helper, him the crowner, at last to account him the reward, to expect from him no other than himself. If thou lovest, love freely. If thou truly lovest, let him whom thou lovest be himself the reward. *And depth.* Of charity, that is, that you may be able to understand the hidden judgment of God; why he gives to this man, but not indeed to that. For from the depth of the judgments of God, which we cannot search out and contemplate, proceeds all that we can. What I can, I see; whence I can, I do not see; except that I know it is from God. But why he should give to that man, and not give to this, is far from me, it is an abyss and a depth. Now therefore charity itself is exercised in good works for the succouring of others, and is extended even to enemies; and this is breadth. Now with longanimity it bears adversities, and perseveres in that which it has truly held; and this is length. But all this it does for the obtaining of the eternal country, which is promised to it on high; and this is height. But that charity arises out of the hidden, and this is depth.

*That you may be filled.* Because then nothing is lacking to the Christian, when he thus knows the Father and the Son. Otherwise the profession of the deity is not entire, because faith is neither entire in the Father alone, nor perfect in the Son alone. *Unto all the fullness of God.* Not that they be (full God) as certain erring men have wished, but that they be perfectly filled with God; or thus: that by confession and thanksgiving honour be reserved to the Son as to the Father, and that all things which are from God the Father be believed to have been made and restored through the Son, that there may be a full profession of the divinity in believers.
*He is able to do all things,* etc. In this are certain things which otherwise no one would ask or understand, as that God should die as man for men, and other things of this kind.

notes.text: After these things — The history of between ten and eleven months is to be supplied here from the other evangelists. Matt. xiv, 13; Mark vi, 32; Luke ix, 10.
Jesus went up — Before the people overtook him.
Jesus saith to Philip — Perhaps he had the care of providing victuals for the family of the apostles.
He retired to the mountain alone — Having ordered his disciples to cross over the lake.
Matt. xiv, 22; Mark vi, 45.

glossa.text: *Beyond the sea.* Tiberias and Capharnaum are upon the same shore, on our side; beyond, upon the other shore opposite, is the place where that miracle was done. Nor is it properly called a sea, but a certain great overflowing of the Jordan.

*And there followed.* This miracle having been seen, a great crowd of the nations follows, because, as the spirit within restored those whom he was healing from infirmity of the body, so he was healing these same men from the disease of unbelief.

*When he had lifted up.* By his own example he admonishes us to lift up the eyes of our heart, that if perchance, under his leading, we are permitted to ascend to the height of action and of knowledge, the crowd of carnal thoughts that follow may not disturb us, nor cast us down from the height of contemplation, but that we may take care to feed it with spiritual food, as much as it can take.

*Of two hundred.* The number of a hundred doubled signifies the perfection of good action and of rational knowledge, which do not suffice for those who are to be instructed in the faith, unless the height of theology be added to them, which leads souls purged by good working and enlightened by the knowledge of created things to the consummated fullness of spiritual refreshments.

*There is one boy.* This boy is Moses the lawgiver, whose law brought no one to perfection. One, because he prefigured the future vanity *vanitatem*; read *unitatem*, "the unity" of the Church. Here, that is, in the Old Testament, which, although it now grows cheap as the New shines out, has nevertheless not altogether withdrawn. *But these,* etc. As if he should say: The letter of the law, or the bodily senses, what do they profit toward the multitude of those who believe in thee, who are about to ask for spiritual nourishments, which surpass every letter and every bodily sense?

*Make the men.* The Master of truth first instructed his hearers in the simplicity of the letter, as in the lowest places, and in the simplicity of the visible creature, that so they might be raised up to the height of contemplation.

*Those men therefore, when they had seen that,* etc. They were not yet advancing in full faith, wherefore they knew not how to call him God. We, more certain than they, say: This is the Word, without whom there is no prophet or angel.

*Jesus therefore.* They who wish to take him by force and to make him king signify the disciples and the other believers, who wish to anticipate the time of his kingdom, thinking that he had come in such wise that he should already reign. But in this time the kingdom is being gathered, which at the end will be made manifest, when he shall say: *Receive the kingdom which is prepared for you.* He flees therefore, not fearing to be held, he who afterwards converses with those same men, but wishing to signify that his height cannot be understood. He flees into the mountain, that is, he ascends the heavens, alone a priest interceding for the people set outside, who meanwhile is tossed by the waves; whence he adds: *But when evening was come.* The evening of the world is after the ascension of Christ, in which the disciples go down to the labours of the world, and steer the ship, that is, the Church.

*They were afraid.* That the disciples, who bore the figure of all who were to be in the Church, when they had seen the Lord coming to them upon the wave of the sea, were afraid, and, as another evangelist says more openly, believed him a phantasm, is not void of mystery, because even to this day many in the Church, when they hear themselves urged to let go present and perishable goods for the sake of eternal ones, whatsoever they are to have, are afraid and believe themselves deceived; to whom the Lord says: *Fear not, it is I.*

When the storms of life are raging, stand by me

echoes.text: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: 'Rooted and grounded in love' draws on the OT image of the person planted by water who is 'rooted' and bears fruit (Jeremiah 17:8; cf. Psalm 1:3). The agricultural 'rooted' metaphor for the secure, flourishing believer is the same, giving good coherence; the architectural 'grounded' pairs a building image, but the rootedness half is a clear OT echo.

echoes.text: “Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty? They are high as heaven. What can you do? They are deeper than Sheol. What can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.
echoes.note: 'The breadth and length and height and depth' that the saints 'comprehend' echoes Job 11:7-9, where the unsearchable extent of God is measured by 'higher than heaven... deeper than Sheol... longer than the earth and broader than the sea.' The four-dimensional measuring of an immeasurable divine reality is a distinctive shared template, giving good coherence even without verbatim wording.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: 'I bow my knees to the Father' evokes the universal-homage motif of Isaiah 45:23, 'to me every knee shall bow,' the OT locus for bending the knee to God. The posture and the universal-fatherhood frame ('every family in heaven and on earth') cohere, though the volume of the verbal link is faint here.

echoes.text: It was so, that when Solomon had made an end of praying all this prayer and supplication to Yahweh, he arose from before the altar of Yahweh, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.
echoes.note: Bowing the knees to the Father in intercessory prayer recalls Solomon kneeling with hands spread to heaven in dedicatory prayer (1 Kings 8:54; cf. Ezra 9:5; Daniel 6:10). The kneeling-in-prayer gesture is a shared OT posture, supporting a faint echo rather than a pointed allusion.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: Psalm 1:3's 'tree planted by streams of water' that flourishes is the classic OT picture of the rooted, stable righteous person and reinforces 'rooted and grounded in love.' It is best paired with Jeremiah 17:8 as part of the same planted-tree image cluster rather than an independent source.

echoes.text: The height of the heaven, and the breadth of the earth, And the deep, and wisdom, who shall search them out?
echoes.note: The same four-dimensional immeasurability motif appears in Sirach 1:3, 'the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, the deep, and wisdom — who can search them out?' applied to God's wisdom. Within Second-Temple wisdom literature this strengthens the availability of the breadth/length/height/depth topos behind verse 18.

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: The doxology 'to him be the glory... forever and ever' draws on David's blessing, 'Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory... yours is the kingdom... forever.' The pattern of ascribing glory and power to God in an everlasting public blessing is the OT model for this doxology; coherence is high, the link being formal rather than verbatim.

echoes.text: Praise be to Yahweh God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds. Blessed be his glorious name forever! Let the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and amen.
echoes.note: 'To him be the glory... to all generations forever and ever. Amen' closely matches the closing doxology of Psalm 72:18-19, 'blessed be his glorious name forever... Amen and Amen,' which praises the God 'who alone does wondrous things.' The wondrous-deeds-plus-eternal-glory-plus-Amen structure makes this a strong formal model, supporting medium confidence.

echoes.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised! His greatness is unsearchable.
echoes.note: 'Him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think' coheres with Psalm 145:3, 'great is the Lord and greatly to be praised; his greatness is unsearchable,' which celebrates God's measureless power as ground for praise. The link is conceptual (immeasurable divine ability) rather than verbal, hence a faint echo.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'Able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think' echoes the OT confession that nothing is too hard/wonderful for the Lord (Genesis 18:14; cf. Jeremiah 32:17,27). The motif of God's unlimited capacity to do what humans cannot conceive coheres, but the volume is low and it is one of several possible backgrounds.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The wilderness feeding of a great multitude with miraculous bread sets the controlling type that the chapter will name explicitly in v.31. High Volume and total Coherence with the manna economy (bread, gathering, leftovers, no waste); the feeding scene is the narrative enactment of the manna gift Jesus later interprets.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Philip's 'Where are we to buy bread... not sufficient' (v.7) closely mirrors Moses' despairing 'Where am I to get meat... shall flocks and herds be slaughtered to suffice them?' Strong structural and verbal Coherence: a leader confronted with an impossible crowd, mountain setting, and divine provision overriding human arithmetic.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha multiplies twenty barley loaves to feed a hundred with leftovers, dismissing a servant's 'How can I set this before a hundred?' John alone specifies 'barley loaves' and 'what are these among so many?', and adds the leftovers motif. High Volume and verbal Recurrence make this the closest single OT analogue to the miracle's mechanics.

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.
echoes.note: Asaph's 'he rained down manna... gave them grain of heaven... bread of the angels' is the psalm John will quote at v.31; its presence governs the feeding as the eschatological manna. High Coherence: the crowd reads the sign as a renewed wilderness banquet.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world' (v.14) invokes the promised prophet-like-Moses. The Mosaic feeding miracle triggers a Mosaic-prophet expectation; high Coherence with John's prophet-and-king Christology.

echoes.text: They asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of the sky.
echoes.note: 'He gave them bread from heaven in abundance' — a second psalmic celebration of the manna, reinforcing the satisfied-fullness motif ('when they were filled,' v.12). Lower distinctiveness than Ps 78 but adds Recurrence to the manna tradition active here.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John's editorial note 'Now the Passover was at hand' (v.4) frames the whole chapter under the paschal lamb, preparing the flesh-and-blood discourse (vv.51-56). Availability and Coherence are strong; the Passover anchor is authorial, though the feeding scene itself does not verbally cite Exodus 12.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance. Moses alone shall come near to Yahweh, but they shall not come near, neither shall the people go up with him.” Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.” Moses wrote all Yahweh’s […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'went up into the mountain and sat there with his disciples' (v.3) before a meal faintly recalls Moses ascending Sinai where the elders 'beheld God and ate and drank.' Suggestive of a covenant-meal-on-the-mountain pattern but low Volume; contested.

echoes.text: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to Yahweh. Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.
echoes.note: The crowd's move to 'take him by force, to make him king' (v.15) faintly evokes Israel's improper demand for a king, which the LORD treats as rejection of his rule. Thematic rather than verbal; offered as a contested background to Jesus' refusal of a politicized kingship.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' 'It is I (ego eimi); do not be afraid' atop the storm reads, in John's idiom, as the divine self-naming 'I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's later absolute 'I am' sayings; the theophanic-on-the-water setting elevates the otherwise ordinary phrase to divine self-disclosure.

echoes.text: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.
echoes.note: 'who alone... treads on the waves of the sea' ascribes sea-trampling to God alone. Jesus 'walking on the sea' enacts a prerogative the OT reserves for the Creator; strong Volume and Coherence with the I-AM disclosure that accompanies it.

echoes.text: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.
echoes.note: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen' — a hymn of God's exodus march across the deep. Coheres with Jesus pathless on the water; the psalm's exodus frame fits John's Passover setting.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you' pairs the precise reassurance ('Don't be afraid') with passage through threatening waters. Coherence with the disciples' deliverance; the chapter's I-AM resonates with Isaiah 43:10 below.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: 'that you may... believe me and understand that I am he (ani hu / ego eimi)' supplies the LXX 'I am' that stands behind Jesus' words on the sea. Strengthens the case that v.20's ego eimi is theophanic rather than mere identification.

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: Seafarers in a wind-tossed storm cry out and God 'made the storm a calm' and 'brought them to their desired haven' — strikingly close to the boat reaching land 'immediately' (v.21). Good Coherence though John gives stilling-by-arrival rather than rebuke of the storm.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left. The Egyptians pursued, and went in after them into the midst of the sea: all of Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. In the […]
echoes.note: Under the Passover frame, a nighttime deliverance over/through the sea recalls the Red Sea crossing where Israel 'feared' then was saved. Typological rather than verbal; coheres with the exodus pattern saturating the chapter.

notes.text: First fruits — Which were the priests due, Num. xviii, 12, but these, and probably the rest of the priests dues, were usually brought by the pious Israelites, according to their ability and opportunity, to the Lord's prophets, because they were not permitted to carry them to Jerusalem. Naaman hears of Elisha, ver. 1-4. The king of Syria sends him to the king of Israel, ver. 5-7. He goes to Elisha and is healed, ver. 8-14. His grateful acknowledgment to Elisha, ver. 15-19. Gehazi follows him, and receives gifts from him, ver. 20-24. The leprosy of Naaman entailed on Gehazi's family, ver. 25-27.

glossa.text: *And a man.* ((RAB.)) The man is the company of the fathers: who is of Baalalisa, because he keeps the number three in the confession of the Trinity. For Baalalisa is interpreted "having a third." This man offers to the man of God loaves of the firstfruits; when, inspired by his grace, he offers to the Redeemer books composed concerning the origin of creatures. He offers new corn in his scrip; when he brings forth the New Testament in the writings of the Gospel and of the apostles. Our Elisaeus bids his ministers, that is, the preachers, dispense these things to the faithful, and bring forth out of their treasure new things and old, which mystery we read in the Gospel in the breaking of the five and of the seven loaves, where, when the multitudes had been filled, they gathered twelve baskets, or seven hampers, of fragments, because no one grasps the sacraments of Scripture in all their parts, since, when he has been filled, there will be left over to him according to the word of the Lord.

notes.text: All — All that look up to him for help.
All — Of all living creatures. Wait - Expect their supplies wholly from thy bounty. Expectation is here figuratively ascribed to brute creatures.

Nigh — To answer their prayers. In truth - With an upright heart. The psalmist praises God, and exhorts all to trust in him alone, ver. 1-5. Because of his power, faithfulness and everlasting kingdom, ver. 6-10.

glossa.text:
*Let all thy works confess to thee, O Lord.* ((AUG.)) Let them praise as do those things which have not the sense of praising, which are the matter of praise: because while thou inquirest, thou findest a great power in them, which is from God.

*And thy saints.* ((CAS.)) Everything that is confesses either by itself, or through rational creatures. Or the saints, that is, angels and men. This concerning holiness: for this is the holiness of God, that the saints should owe him confession.
*The glory of the kingdom.* ((ID.)) It is taken therefore from the wonders. As if: How wonderful is he who made heaven and earth, and filled them with divers good things.
*That known.* ((ID.)) This is taken from the power of terrible things, etc., *as far as* to whom, being magnificent, nothing is compared.

*Thy kingdom,* etc. ((ID.)) He praises from the perpetuity and the effect of dominion. And this is taken from greatness: if it is great to rule for a time, it is greater to have no term of dominion.

*The Lord is faithful in all.* ((ID.)) This is taken from the abundant sweetness; whence above: *The memory of the abundance of thy sweetness. Faithful,* because his coming fulfilled the gifts. To abundance also belongs that he lifts up those who fall, raises up the crushed; whence the remembrance of sweetness is had, and is belched forth in his praises.

*Who fall down.* ((CAS.)) From their own evils, all of whom God lifts up. Or, from these temporal things, as the saints do, like Job, who lose something in the world and are made abject, and are falling: but all these he confirms, because seven times the just man falls and rises again; but the wicked are weakened in evils ((Prov. XXIV)).

*And he lifts up all that are cast down.* ((AUG.)) Those belonging to him, because he resists the proud.

*The eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord.* ((ID.)) He treats of justice at greater length, that he who hears of the merciful one may fear the just one: and it belongs to justice that he should satisfy those who hope, bodily or spiritually. For food is not always to be given, but in due season: for to many who ask it is wholesomely deferred. *And thou givest them their food in due season.* ((ID.)) The physician therefore gives the sick man what is fitting, etc., *as far as* blessing God at all times.
*Thou openest the hand.* ((ID.)) Although sometimes thou dost not give, yet thou givest opportunely: thou deferrest indeed, thou dost not take away.

*Just.* ((CAS.)) By the very name he discloses justice, that it may be manifestly shown that this praise is concerning justice. *Ways* are dispositions and wills, which are all just, even if he scourges.

*In his ways, and holy in all* *omnibns* *his works.* It is to be known that *Ways* pertain to disposition, works to effect: these are divided according to us. But with him, to will is the same as to do: because from his will things have their being.
*He is near to all that call upon him.* ((CAS.)) Propitious, who is everywhere, and this concerning justice.

notes.text: Of whom — The Father. The whole family of angels in heaven, saints in paradise, and believers on earth is named. Being the "children of God," (a more honourable title than "children of Abraham,") and depending on him as the Father of the family.
The riches of his glory — The immense fulness of his glorious wisdom, power, and mercy. The inner man - The soul.
Dwell — That is, constantly and sensibly abide.

That being rooted and grounded — That is, deeply fixed and firmly established, in love. Ye may comprehend - So far as an human mind is capable. What is the breadth of the love of Christ - Embracing all mankind. And length - From everlasting to everlasting. And depth - Not to be fathomed by any creature. And height - Not to be reached by any enemy.

And to know — But the apostle corrects himself, and immediately observes, it cannot be fully known. This only we know, that the love of Christ surpasses all knowledge. That ye may be filled - Which is the sum of all. With all the fulness of God - With all his light, love, wisdom, holiness, power, and glory. A perfection far beyond a bare freedom from sin.

Now to him — This doxology is admirably adapted to strengthen our faith, that we may not stagger at the great things the apostle has been praying for, as if they were too much for God to give, or for us to expect from him. That is able - Here is a most beautiful gradation. When he has given us exceeding, yea, abundant blessings, still we may ask for more. And he is able to do it. But we may think of more than we have asked. He is able to do this also. Yea, and above all this. Above all we ask - Above all we can think. Nay, exceedingly, abundantly above all that we can either ask or think.
In the church — On earth and in heaven.

glossa.text: *For this cause.* I entreat you, and I beseech God, that grace may work together with you. And this is what he adds: *For this cause.* In which he shows that they have the free choice of their own will. But lest they think that this suffices, he adds: *I bow my knees to the Father.* So much only is had in the Greek; but what has been added in the Latin codices: *of our Lord Jesus Christ,* fits well, in that he was praying that we might obtain by the merit of him to whom he is Father properly and naturally, and not by adoption.

*Fatherhood,* etc. Neither angel, nor man is truly a father as God is, who is the father of all by creation, and of the faithful by re-creation, whom he adopted as sons. Or *is named,* that is, is nameable. For from him who is the father of all, both the angels in heaven and men on earth received that they should call others fathers. And note that Christ, the only-begotten of God by nature, signifies by the benefit of adoption that he is a father, saying, *Son, thy sins are forgiven thee ((Matth. II))*. In like manner also the Holy Spirit, through whom the just are adopted as sons. But a man is called father either by nature, or by the authority of example, or by reason of benefit.
*In charity.* I pray also that [you may be] *rooted,* that is, firmly planted, from the likeness of a tree, which the more it is fixed in the earth, the more it grows, and yields a richer fruit.

*With all the saints.* This is the communion of the heavenly commonwealth. These seek not their own, but the things which are Christ's, that is, they pursue not private advantages, but take counsel in the communion where the salvation of all is.

*What is the breadth.* Of charity, which ought to be extended even to enemies, and to work well with cheerfulness, because he who gives sadly loses what he gives. There is need, therefore, of the breadth of charity, lest whatever good thou dost should perish. But because, iniquity abounding, the charity of many grows cold, there is need also of length.

*And sublimity.* Of charity. This is that the heart be directed upward, that God be awaited as the reward. For if thou workest well even toward enemies, and givest cheerfully, thou hast breadth; and if in these things unto the end thou perseverest, thou hast length. But if thou do all these things not for the sake of the heavenly reward, it has not height: and so now there will be neither breadth nor length. For to have height is to think God, to love God, and freely to love him the helper, him the crowner, at last to account him the reward, to expect from him no other than himself. If thou lovest, love freely. If thou truly lovest, let him whom thou lovest be himself the reward. *And depth.* Of charity, that is, that you may be able to understand the hidden judgment of God; why he gives to this man, but not indeed to that. For from the depth of the judgments of God, which we cannot search out and contemplate, proceeds all that we can. What I can, I see; whence I can, I do not see; except that I know it is from God. But why he should give to that man, and not give to this, is far from me, it is an abyss and a depth. Now therefore charity itself is exercised in good works for the succouring of others, and is extended even to enemies; and this is breadth. Now with longanimity it bears adversities, and perseveres in that which it has truly held; and this is length. But all this it does for the obtaining of the eternal country, which is promised to it on high; and this is height. But that charity arises out of the hidden, and this is depth.

*That you may be filled.* Because then nothing is lacking to the Christian, when he thus knows the Father and the Son. Otherwise the profession of the deity is not entire, because faith is neither entire in the Father alone, nor perfect in the Son alone. *Unto all the fullness of God.* Not that they be (full God) as certain erring men have wished, but that they be perfectly filled with God; or thus: that by confession and thanksgiving honour be reserved to the Son as to the Father, and that all things which are from God the Father be believed to have been made and restored through the Son, that there may be a full profession of the divinity in believers.
*He is able to do all things,* etc. In this are certain things which otherwise no one would ask or understand, as that God should die as man for men, and other things of this kind.

notes.text: After these things — The history of between ten and eleven months is to be supplied here from the other evangelists. Matt. xiv, 13; Mark vi, 32; Luke ix, 10.
Jesus went up — Before the people overtook him.
Jesus saith to Philip — Perhaps he had the care of providing victuals for the family of the apostles.
He retired to the mountain alone — Having ordered his disciples to cross over the lake.
Matt. xiv, 22; Mark vi, 45.

glossa.text: *Beyond the sea.* Tiberias and Capharnaum are upon the same shore, on our side; beyond, upon the other shore opposite, is the place where that miracle was done. Nor is it properly called a sea, but a certain great overflowing of the Jordan.

*And there followed.* This miracle having been seen, a great crowd of the nations follows, because, as the spirit within restored those whom he was healing from infirmity of the body, so he was healing these same men from the disease of unbelief.

*When he had lifted up.* By his own example he admonishes us to lift up the eyes of our heart, that if perchance, under his leading, we are permitted to ascend to the height of action and of knowledge, the crowd of carnal thoughts that follow may not disturb us, nor cast us down from the height of contemplation, but that we may take care to feed it with spiritual food, as much as it can take.

*Of two hundred.* The number of a hundred doubled signifies the perfection of good action and of rational knowledge, which do not suffice for those who are to be instructed in the faith, unless the height of theology be added to them, which leads souls purged by good working and enlightened by the knowledge of created things to the consummated fullness of spiritual refreshments.

*There is one boy.* This boy is Moses the lawgiver, whose law brought no one to perfection. One, because he prefigured the future vanity *vanitatem*; read *unitatem*, "the unity" of the Church. Here, that is, in the Old Testament, which, although it now grows cheap as the New shines out, has nevertheless not altogether withdrawn. *But these,* etc. As if he should say: The letter of the law, or the bodily senses, what do they profit toward the multitude of those who believe in thee, who are about to ask for spiritual nourishments, which surpass every letter and every bodily sense?

*Make the men.* The Master of truth first instructed his hearers in the simplicity of the letter, as in the lowest places, and in the simplicity of the visible creature, that so they might be raised up to the height of contemplation.

*Those men therefore, when they had seen that,* etc. They were not yet advancing in full faith, wherefore they knew not how to call him God. We, more certain than they, say: This is the Word, without whom there is no prophet or angel.

*Jesus therefore.* They who wish to take him by force and to make him king signify the disciples and the other believers, who wish to anticipate the time of his kingdom, thinking that he had come in such wise that he should already reign. But in this time the kingdom is being gathered, which at the end will be made manifest, when he shall say: *Receive the kingdom which is prepared for you.* He flees therefore, not fearing to be held, he who afterwards converses with those same men, but wishing to signify that his height cannot be understood. He flees into the mountain, that is, he ascends the heavens, alone a priest interceding for the people set outside, who meanwhile is tossed by the waves; whence he adds: *But when evening was come.* The evening of the world is after the ascension of Christ, in which the disciples go down to the labours of the world, and steer the ship, that is, the Church.

*They were afraid.* That the disciples, who bore the figure of all who were to be in the Church, when they had seen the Lord coming to them upon the wave of the sea, were afraid, and, as another evangelist says more openly, believed him a phantasm, is not void of mystery, because even to this day many in the Church, when they hear themselves urged to let go present and perishable goods for the sake of eternal ones, whatsoever they are to have, are afraid and believe themselves deceived; to whom the Lord says: *Fear not, it is I.*

echoes.text: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: 'Rooted and grounded in love' draws on the OT image of the person planted by water who is 'rooted' and bears fruit (Jeremiah 17:8; cf. Psalm 1:3). The agricultural 'rooted' metaphor for the secure, flourishing believer is the same, giving good coherence; the architectural 'grounded' pairs a building image, but the rootedness half is a clear OT echo.

echoes.text: “Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty? They are high as heaven. What can you do? They are deeper than Sheol. What can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.
echoes.note: 'The breadth and length and height and depth' that the saints 'comprehend' echoes Job 11:7-9, where the unsearchable extent of God is measured by 'higher than heaven... deeper than Sheol... longer than the earth and broader than the sea.' The four-dimensional measuring of an immeasurable divine reality is a distinctive shared template, giving good coherence even without verbatim wording.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: 'I bow my knees to the Father' evokes the universal-homage motif of Isaiah 45:23, 'to me every knee shall bow,' the OT locus for bending the knee to God. The posture and the universal-fatherhood frame ('every family in heaven and on earth') cohere, though the volume of the verbal link is faint here.

echoes.text: It was so, that when Solomon had made an end of praying all this prayer and supplication to Yahweh, he arose from before the altar of Yahweh, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.
echoes.note: Bowing the knees to the Father in intercessory prayer recalls Solomon kneeling with hands spread to heaven in dedicatory prayer (1 Kings 8:54; cf. Ezra 9:5; Daniel 6:10). The kneeling-in-prayer gesture is a shared OT posture, supporting a faint echo rather than a pointed allusion.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: Psalm 1:3's 'tree planted by streams of water' that flourishes is the classic OT picture of the rooted, stable righteous person and reinforces 'rooted and grounded in love.' It is best paired with Jeremiah 17:8 as part of the same planted-tree image cluster rather than an independent source.

echoes.text: The height of the heaven, and the breadth of the earth, And the deep, and wisdom, who shall search them out?
echoes.note: The same four-dimensional immeasurability motif appears in Sirach 1:3, 'the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, the deep, and wisdom — who can search them out?' applied to God's wisdom. Within Second-Temple wisdom literature this strengthens the availability of the breadth/length/height/depth topos behind verse 18.

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: The doxology 'to him be the glory... forever and ever' draws on David's blessing, 'Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory... yours is the kingdom... forever.' The pattern of ascribing glory and power to God in an everlasting public blessing is the OT model for this doxology; coherence is high, the link being formal rather than verbatim.

echoes.text: Praise be to Yahweh God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds. Blessed be his glorious name forever! Let the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and amen.
echoes.note: 'To him be the glory... to all generations forever and ever. Amen' closely matches the closing doxology of Psalm 72:18-19, 'blessed be his glorious name forever... Amen and Amen,' which praises the God 'who alone does wondrous things.' The wondrous-deeds-plus-eternal-glory-plus-Amen structure makes this a strong formal model, supporting medium confidence.

echoes.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised! His greatness is unsearchable.
echoes.note: 'Him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think' coheres with Psalm 145:3, 'great is the Lord and greatly to be praised; his greatness is unsearchable,' which celebrates God's measureless power as ground for praise. The link is conceptual (immeasurable divine ability) rather than verbal, hence a faint echo.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'Able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think' echoes the OT confession that nothing is too hard/wonderful for the Lord (Genesis 18:14; cf. Jeremiah 32:17,27). The motif of God's unlimited capacity to do what humans cannot conceive coheres, but the volume is low and it is one of several possible backgrounds.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The wilderness feeding of a great multitude with miraculous bread sets the controlling type that the chapter will name explicitly in v.31. High Volume and total Coherence with the manna economy (bread, gathering, leftovers, no waste); the feeding scene is the narrative enactment of the manna gift Jesus later interprets.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Philip's 'Where are we to buy bread... not sufficient' (v.7) closely mirrors Moses' despairing 'Where am I to get meat... shall flocks and herds be slaughtered to suffice them?' Strong structural and verbal Coherence: a leader confronted with an impossible crowd, mountain setting, and divine provision overriding human arithmetic.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha multiplies twenty barley loaves to feed a hundred with leftovers, dismissing a servant's 'How can I set this before a hundred?' John alone specifies 'barley loaves' and 'what are these among so many?', and adds the leftovers motif. High Volume and verbal Recurrence make this the closest single OT analogue to the miracle's mechanics.

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.
echoes.note: Asaph's 'he rained down manna... gave them grain of heaven... bread of the angels' is the psalm John will quote at v.31; its presence governs the feeding as the eschatological manna. High Coherence: the crowd reads the sign as a renewed wilderness banquet.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world' (v.14) invokes the promised prophet-like-Moses. The Mosaic feeding miracle triggers a Mosaic-prophet expectation; high Coherence with John's prophet-and-king Christology.

echoes.text: They asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of the sky.
echoes.note: 'He gave them bread from heaven in abundance' — a second psalmic celebration of the manna, reinforcing the satisfied-fullness motif ('when they were filled,' v.12). Lower distinctiveness than Ps 78 but adds Recurrence to the manna tradition active here.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John's editorial note 'Now the Passover was at hand' (v.4) frames the whole chapter under the paschal lamb, preparing the flesh-and-blood discourse (vv.51-56). Availability and Coherence are strong; the Passover anchor is authorial, though the feeding scene itself does not verbally cite Exodus 12.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance. Moses alone shall come near to Yahweh, but they shall not come near, neither shall the people go up with him.” Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.” Moses wrote all Yahweh’s […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'went up into the mountain and sat there with his disciples' (v.3) before a meal faintly recalls Moses ascending Sinai where the elders 'beheld God and ate and drank.' Suggestive of a covenant-meal-on-the-mountain pattern but low Volume; contested.

echoes.text: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to Yahweh. Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.
echoes.note: The crowd's move to 'take him by force, to make him king' (v.15) faintly evokes Israel's improper demand for a king, which the LORD treats as rejection of his rule. Thematic rather than verbal; offered as a contested background to Jesus' refusal of a politicized kingship.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' 'It is I (ego eimi); do not be afraid' atop the storm reads, in John's idiom, as the divine self-naming 'I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's later absolute 'I am' sayings; the theophanic-on-the-water setting elevates the otherwise ordinary phrase to divine self-disclosure.

echoes.text: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.
echoes.note: 'who alone... treads on the waves of the sea' ascribes sea-trampling to God alone. Jesus 'walking on the sea' enacts a prerogative the OT reserves for the Creator; strong Volume and Coherence with the I-AM disclosure that accompanies it.

echoes.text: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.
echoes.note: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen' — a hymn of God's exodus march across the deep. Coheres with Jesus pathless on the water; the psalm's exodus frame fits John's Passover setting.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you' pairs the precise reassurance ('Don't be afraid') with passage through threatening waters. Coherence with the disciples' deliverance; the chapter's I-AM resonates with Isaiah 43:10 below.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: 'that you may... believe me and understand that I am he (ani hu / ego eimi)' supplies the LXX 'I am' that stands behind Jesus' words on the sea. Strengthens the case that v.20's ego eimi is theophanic rather than mere identification.

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: Seafarers in a wind-tossed storm cry out and God 'made the storm a calm' and 'brought them to their desired haven' — strikingly close to the boat reaching land 'immediately' (v.21). Good Coherence though John gives stilling-by-arrival rather than rebuke of the storm.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left. The Egyptians pursued, and went in after them into the midst of the sea: all of Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. In the […]
echoes.note: Under the Passover frame, a nighttime deliverance over/through the sea recalls the Red Sea crossing where Israel 'feared' then was saved. Typological rather than verbal; coheres with the exodus pattern saturating the chapter.

registers.label: Spare
lines: A boy brings five loaves and two fish to a hungry crowd.
And in the hands of Jesus, little becomes more than enough.
They ate, all five thousand, and the baskets ran over.
God spreads a table where we saw only lack.
Across the dark water a voice: It is I; do not be afraid.
We will not fear; the Lord is in the boat.
Come, let us worship the God who feeds us.
We come hungry, and we are filled. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Five thousand people on a green hillside, and nothing but a boy's lunch, five barley loaves and two small fish, passed into the hands of Jesus.
Give us this bread always.
He gives thanks and breaks it, and it keeps coming, basket after basket, until everyone has eaten their fill and twelve baskets are left over.
Give us this bread always.
Night falls, the wind comes up, the disciples strain at the oars, and across the black water he walks, saying, It is I; do not be afraid.
Give us this bread always.
So bring your little here, your not-enough; in the hands of Jesus it will feed the whole hungry crowd of you.
Give us this bread always.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Five loaves, two fish, and a hillside of hungry people.
Give us this bread always.
He breaks it, and the baskets overflow.
Give us this bread always.
Across the dark water: It is I; do not be afraid.
Give us this bread always.
Come, let us worship the God who feeds us.
Give us this bread always. Amen.
